title: Thirty Minutes on Sunday That Buy Back a Week
body: I have attempted the weekly review six or seven times in my life, the way other people attempt jogging. Enthusiastically, with equipment, for about three weeks. The pattern of failure was always the same. The first review took two hours and felt like organizing a warehouse. The second took ninety minutes. By the fourth I was skimming my own lists with the energy of a man reading terms and conditions, and by the fifth Sunday the habit was gone, and I felt the specific shame of a person who has disappointed a system of their own design. What changed was not discipline. It was scope. The reviews that failed were reviews of everything. The review that stuck is a review of exactly one question, asked three ways, in thirty minutes, on Sunday evening, with tea. The question is this. Where did the week actually go. Way one. I open the calendar and read it like a stranger. Where did the blocks go, and were they the blocks I chose. This takes eight minutes and is regularly humiliating. Two meetings I could have declined. One afternoon that evaporated into what my calendar politely calls focus time and what I remember as scrolling. Way two. I look at one list, the one called waiting, where I keep everything I promised other people. Anything sitting there more than two weeks gets either done this week or confessed this week. Confession is allowed. Silent rot is not. This takes six minutes and it has saved more relationships than any communication advice I have ever read. People do not actually mind waiting. They mind not knowing they are waiting. Way three. I ask where the money and the energy went, together, because they leak through the same holes. Subscriptions I forgot, groceries that became delivery, evenings that became screens. Not a budget review. A leak review. Ten minutes, two columns, one line each for the biggest leak of the week. Then the card for Monday gets written, three lines, and the review is over. If the tea is still warm, I did it right. The unexpected benefit was not organization. It was fairness. Before the review, my weeks felt like they happened to me. After a month of reviews, the weeks became things I could describe, and a week you can describe is a week you can negotiate with. I stopped calling myself lazy on Sunday nights, because the record showed something more accurate. I was not lazy. I was unscheduled in specific, repeatable places. The failure mode now is different and milder. Some Sundays the review becomes a prosecution and I leave with a list of eleven resolutions, which is the review overreaching. The rule that catches this is that the review produces exactly one change for the coming week. One. If the week's record was bad, one change. If it was good, one change. A system that demands eleven improvements a week is not a system, it is a revenge fantasy. Thirty minutes. One question, asked three ways. One change. My grandfather, who ran his shop for forty years on a wall calendar and a pencil, would have found the whole thing obvious. He would also have noted that I needed a notebook, a timer, and six failed attempts to learn what he knew at fifteen. He would be right. He usually was.
